Everything an operator can change is in the database, and most of it is on these pages. The listeners, TLS and the database connection are the exception: those are read when the server starts, and the About page says which ones a change is waiting on.
No IPv6, so publish only an A record. Some large providers prefer IPv6 but none require it.
Large receivers decide on these three before reading a single header. Nothing here is about how mail reaches you: it is what a receiver sees when this server reaches out.
How your outgoing mail identifies itself

Outgoing mail leaves through your proxy, so these are the proxy\'s address and what it looks like from outside, not the address mail arrives at. Large receivers decide on these three before reading a single header.
Leave these empty to follow the server name and the ports it listens on. Fill them in when a router or a container takes the usual port on the outside and forwards it to a different one here.

The reverse name is %1$s, but it resolves to %2$s rather than %3$s, so the confirmation fails and receivers treat the mail as unverified. Publish an A record for %1$s pointing at %3$s, or change the reverse name to one that already does.

This address has no reverse name, and many receivers refuse mail from an address that has none. Set it where the address is managed (at a cloud provider that is the address\'s own setting in the console or API, not a DNS record), then publish an A record for that name pointing at %1$s.
The address a phone or a mail program should connect to when sending through this server, with STARTTLS. It is what the credential dialog shows.
